errors.why: ཚངས་པ here (= ཚང་བ) means 'complete/full', i.e. the Vinaya complete enough to carry out motions and formal acts, not 'pure'.

note: Faithful rendering of the verses and the commentary on the Vinaya's praise; one doubtful gloss on 'complete'.

errors.why: ཆོས་ཀྱི་མཆོག is the fourth stage of the path of joining (laukikāgradharma, 'supreme mundane dharma'), continuing the warmth/peak/patience series, not 'supreme qualities'.

fix.replace: At the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma),

errors.english: abandoning faulty discipline and so forth depends on wishing for bodily perfection and other virtues
errors.why: The Tibetan says that, faulty discipline having been abandoned, bodily perfection and the like depend only on one's wish (hence a wish-granting vase); the English inverts the dependence.

fix.find: abandoning faulty discipline and so forth depends on wishing for bodily perfection and other virtues
fix.replace: since faulty discipline and the like have been abandoned, bodily perfection and the like depend only on one's wish

note: The polemic against the other commentators is well handled, but the path-stage simile list mistranslates the supreme-dharma stage and inverts the vase simile.

errors.english: Taking heart from what his dear friend had shown him, the elder brother, possessing keen intellect,
errors.why: The Sanskrit/Tibetan say the brahmin (agrajaḥ, 'first-born' = brahmin) gave courage to his affectionate friend and then went off; agraja is not 'elder brother' and it is the friend who receives the encouragement.

fix.find: Taking heart from what his dear friend had shown him, the elder brother, possessing keen intellect,
fix.replace: Having thus given heart to his dear friend, the brahmin, possessing keen intellect,

errors.english: Adorned with garments and flower garlands under the guise of an auspicious deity, he carried it
errors.why: It is the image that is adorned with garlands and cloth and disguised with a deity's marks, not the brahmin carrying it.

errors.english: a maiden is given only after careful consideration of wealth and diligence
errors.why: 'With effort' (prayatnena) qualifies the careful inquiry into wealth; diligence is not a second criterion.

note: The narrative is followed, but the opening verse misidentifies the brahmin as an elder brother and reverses who encourages whom.

errors.english: Thinking that the experienced object cannot be denied, other opponents demonstrate
errors.why: The clause anticipates what others might think; it is the root text ("the mere seeing of it") that then shows the sequence of engagement, not the opponents.

note: A careful rendering of the pramāṇa/apramāṇa debate on attainment, familiarity and mutual dependence.

errors.english: if that [note: the entity] does not exist
errors.why: 'That' refers back to the non-connection with impermanence (the entity's abiding) from the previous side, not to the entity itself; the note makes the argument incoherent.

note: The argument against sequential and simultaneous arising and destruction and the kṛtaka/akṛtaka dilemma are rendered accurately.

errors.why: དམ་བཅས་པ here is the pledge/convention (samaya) fixed by the powerful author of the mantra, which the next side calls བརྡ, not a debater's thesis.

note: The anti-apauruṣeya argument is followed correctly throughout.

errors.english: yet it is not merely an ordinary emanation
errors.why: The Tibetan says the mind-made body is to be seen as like an emanation but is not an emanation; 'merely an ordinary' weakens the denial.

note: A sound rendering of the mind-made body passage and its scriptural citations (Śrīmālā, Prajñāpāramitā, Laṅkāvatāra).

errors.english: the possession of any goods resting upon it is established by that mat itself
errors.why: The rule concerns the 'place' (གནས) from which removal constitutes theft: the place of goods lying on a spread mat is the mat, not the ground; nothing is said about possession.

fix.find: the possession of any goods resting upon it is established by that mat itself
fix.replace: the place of any goods resting upon it is that mat itself

errors.english: there is no need to doubt that a procedure other than "moving from its place" applies
errors.why: The Tibetan says one should not suspect that the offence arises by a procedure other than moving from place; the English asserts that another procedure does apply.

fix.find: there is no need to doubt that a procedure other than "moving from its place" applies
fix.replace: one should not suspect that the offence arises by a procedure other than "moving from its place"

note: The theft casuistry is mostly followed, but the key notion of 'place' is turned into possession and one sentence on the reading of the root text is inverted.

errors.english: the oval lump [note: original: "nur nur po", *kalala*]
errors.why: ནུར་ནུར་པོ is the second embryonic stage, arbuda (Mvy); kalala is མེར་མེར་པོ.

fix.find: the oval lump [note: original: "nur nur po", *kalala*]
fix.replace: the oval lump [note: original: "nur nur po", *arbuda*]

errors.english: constitutes an occasional cause [note: original: "gnas skabs pa'i rgyu"] or a causal continuum
errors.why: The pair is a cause of a state (avasthā) versus a cause of the continuum, i.e. a cause producing a modification of something versus a cause of its series; neither is 'occasional' nor 'a causal continuum'.

errors.english: only the nature of the effect itself serves as the substantial cause of the occasional and continuous causes
errors.why: The Tibetan says the state- and continuum-causes (fire, clay, etc.) are substantial causes only insofar as they have the nature of the effect; the English makes the effect the substantial cause of those causes.

note: The broad line of the body-mind upādāna argument survives, but the causal terminology and the closing sentence are confused.
A faithful rendering of the Tibetan verses of the Kalpalatā (fratricide and Arthadatta episodes).
